tokyo3_y_28.gf_detail: Real, purpose-built GF items exist: a グルテンフリー塩ラーメン (gluten-free SHIO/salt ramen) using brown-rice noodles from Shimane, developed by the founder specifically with wheat-allergy and celiac diners in mind, plus vegan water-gyoza with a rice-flour wrapper (gluten-free available on request). The Tokyo Station Ichibangai and official listings note staff ask about wheat allergy and cook the GF order in a separate pot — a meaningful positive. HOWEVER this is a small 26-seat counter shop that simultaneously boils regular WHEAT ramen noodles, and the flagship 醤油らーめん is made with 生醤油 (wheat-based raw soy sauce); the standard broths/tsuyu and shared ladles/counter mean cross-contamination is possible. Choose the SHIO (salt) base, not shoyu. This is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen/fryer, so a strict celiac should confirm the separate-pot handling in person on the day and avoid any soy-sauce-based bowl.
tokyo3_y_28.vegan_detail: Several genuinely animal-free dishes: ヴィーガン担々麺 (vegan tantanmen — soy-milk/sesame broth with soy-meat crumbles and chili oil), a vegan veggie-soba (vegetable broth), ヴィーガン水餃子 (vegan water-gyoza, rice-flour wrapper), and a soy-milk soft-serve dessert. IMPORTANT caveats: the popular キノコベジソバ (mushroom veggie-soba) is only vegan when you ORDER IT WITHOUT the 鶏チャーシュー (chicken chashu) and mushroom oil — the default bowl is not vegan. The 貝塩らーめん (clam-salt ramen) is bonito- and shellfish-based — not vegan. Vegan items are served from roughly 10:00. Confirm no dashi/bonito when ordering, since the kitchen also runs animal broths.

chef_bio.background: Founder of the Soranoiro group. Worked at Kumurasaki in the Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum as a university student, then after a company job and a stint at Takechan Niboshi Ramen, joined Hakata Ippudo in March 2000 and trained across many departments for about 10 years 10 months (cooking, store operations, staff development). Opened the first Soranoiro in Kojimachi, Tokyo in June 2011. Now also works as a ramen consultant (frozen-noodle advisor, flour-company advisor, shop production and product development).
chef_bio.philosophy: Mission 'まだ見ぬお客様と業界の発展のために' (for customers yet unseen and the advancement of the industry). Carries the Ippudo principle '変わらないために変わり続けること' (to stay the same you must keep changing). Named the company from the Heart Sutra's 色即是空・空即是色. Sees himself as a chef, not just a ramen-shop operator, and deliberately gives each branch a different menu. Set out to make a ramen shop a woman could enter alone, and built vegetables into the noodles, broth and toppings.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegetable ramen (ベジソバ) — vegetables in the noodles, broth and toppings — plus vegan ramen and a gluten-free (brown-rice-noodle) ramen. The Soranoiro veggie/vegan soba was featured in the Michelin Guide Tokyo (Bib Gourmand, 2015–2017).

anecdotes.text: Trained about 10 years and 10 months at Hakata Ippudo (joined March 2000) before opening the first Soranoiro in Kojimachi in June 2011.
Developed the vegan ramen after a well-received appearance at Paris Ramen Week in 2014, building a vegetable-based broth enriched with carrot and red-pepper puree.

Over ~13 years has created around 300 seasonal limited ramen to connect diners with regional producers nationwide — including sustaining Sanriku seaweed purchases for 8 years to support post-tsunami recovery.

tokyo3_cafe_vava.gf_detail: The signature "VAVAパンケーキ" batter is made with 100% domestic rice flour and, per the official site and menu, uses NO wheat flour (「小麦粉を一切使わない」); it is sweetened with beet sugar (てん菜糖). There is also a gluten-free spaghetti (グルテンフリースパゲッティ, 国産米粉100%: 天使の海老 / アラビアータ). So real, deliberate GF items exist. BUT this is NOT a dedicated gluten-free kitchen: the same menu openly serves wheat-based dishes — モンティクリスト (French toast on bread), 天使の海老バーガー (wheat buns), 天然酵母パン・ド・カンパーニュ (bread), and スコーン. Wheat flour and bread are prepared in the same kitchen, so a strict celiac faces genuine cross-contamination risk (shared surfaces, flour dust, shared griddle/utensils); none of the sources confirm separate prep or a dedicated fryer. Published allergen labels on the GF pancakes note egg (卵), dairy (乳), soy (大豆), shrimp (えび) and yam (山芋). Verdict: the rice-flour pancake and the 米粉 spaghetti are legitimate GF orders, but confirm cross-contamination handling in person — the "gluten-free" branding refers to specific items, not a wheat-free premises.

tokyo3_ginza_49.gf_detail: Not gluten-free and unsafe for a celiac. This is a tempura specialist — every dish is seafood/vegetables deep-fried in a wheat-flour batter (tempura koromo), so wheat is the core of the menu, not incidental. Concrete wheat risks: (1) wheat-flour batter on all fried items plus flour dusting before battering; (2) a single shared frying oil for all tempura (no dedicated GF fryer — cross-contamination with battered items is unavoidable); (3) tentsuyu dipping sauce is a dashi-soy-mirin blend, and standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat; (4) donburi versions (ten-don, kakiage-don) are glazed in the same wheat-soy tare. The rock-salt (岩塩) option only removes the tentsuyu risk — the battered coating still contains wheat. No allergen program, no GF menu, no evidence of GF flour substitution. A celiac should not eat here.
tokyo3_ginza_49.vegan_detail: A vegetable/"vegetarian" tempura course (野菜/ベジタリアン course, ~¥5,500) is listed, so plant-based tempura items exist — but it is not verified vegan and there are hidden animal-product risks. (1) Tempura batter (koromo) traditionally contains egg, which the shop has not confirmed it omits; (2) the tentsuyu dipping sauce is built on dashi, normally katsuobushi (bonito) stock — a hidden fish product; (3) no menu states a vegan/plant-based guarantee. A vegan could potentially eat vegetable tempura dipped in plain rock salt (岩塩 is offered) but must explicitly confirm an egg-free batter and skip the dashi tentsuyu. Treat as "ask; verify egg-free batter + skip dashi sauce."

tokyo3_near_s.gf_detail: Not gluten-free and not suitable for a celiac. This is a traditional Edo soba house: the noodles are a wheat-buckwheat blend (nihachi-style — no juwari/10-wari soba is advertised), so gluten is in the noodle itself. The house tsuyu (dipping/broth) is built on a katsuobushi/soda-katsuo/saba-bushi fish dashi combined with wheat-containing Japanese soy sauce (shoyu). There is no GF menu, no gluten-free soba, and no mention anywhere of allergen handling; a shared soba-boiling pot and shared prep with wheat items make cross-contamination unavoidable. Even a "plain" order would carry wheat via the noodles and the tsuyu. If a celiac still wants to visit, they must call ahead (03-3561-2647) — but treat this as a NO.
tokyo3_near_s.vegan_detail: No vegan menu and animal products are central. The signature dishes are duck (kamo-seiro / kamo course using Saitama domestic aigamo duck), and — critically — the tsuyu and soups on nearly everything are made from a fish-based ichiban dashi (bonito, soda-katsuo, mackerel/saba bushi), so hidden bonito/fish stock is in the "plain" soba broths too. The soba noodles themselves are wheat-and-buckwheat (plant-based as noodles), and there are vegetable side dishes (sakana/otsumami) and sake, but a strict vegan cannot rely on the dipping/broth. Would need to ask for a fish-free preparation, which is not standard here.

chef_bio.background: Ginza Chōjuan was founded in 1935 (Shōwa 10) and is run as a long-standing family soba shop. It belongs to the wider Chōjuan lineage of Edo soba houses that traces to Sōshichi, a Mikawa native who opened the first 'Chōjuan' in Kyōbashi Gorobei-chō around 1702–1704; over generations the master let promising apprentices go independent under the Chōjuan name, which is why many Chōjuan shops exist across Tokyo. This Ginza branch grinds its own buckwheat — grown on the family's own farmland in Hokkaido (Asahikawa) — on a stone mill in-house.
chef_bio.philosophy: House-grown, stone-milled Hokkaido buckwheat paired with a first-run (ichiban) dashi of katsuobushi, soda-katsuo and saba-bushi; the shop is proud of being the originator of kamo-seiro, letting rich domestic duck fat perfume the dipping broth.
chef_bio.specialty: Kamo-seiro (duck seiro) — the dish the shop claims to have invented — using domestic aigamo duck loin and thigh; also regional/craft sake.

anecdotes.text: The shop bills itself as the '90-year-old, birthplace-of-kamo-seiro long-established soba house' (創業90年 鴨せいろ発祥 老舗蕎麦屋).
It grinds buckwheat from its own farmland in Asahikawa, Hokkaido on a stone mill, and finishes dishes with a first dashi of bonito, soda-bonito and mackerel flakes.

The Chōjuan name dates to the Genroku era: Sōshichi came from Mikawa to Edo and opened the original Chōjuan in Kyōbashi around 1702–1704, with the lineage spreading as apprentices were set up under the same noren.

tokyo3_revive_kitchen_three_hibiy.gf_detail: [Held at "ask" 2026-08-20] The description below was not traceable to any source, so the GF label is held down until it is. The kitchen advertises gluten-free options "on request" (per THREE's official page and Tabelog), and there are genuinely rice-based, wheat-free building blocks: the winter-vegetable frittos (フリット) are coated in a 米粉・豆腐の衣 (rice-flour + tofu batter, not wheat tempura batter), and there are rice mains (十穀米/玄米雑穀ご飯). BUT this is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen — it is a shared plant-based kitchen, so a celiac must confirm each dish. Concrete wheat risks found on the menu: the soy-milk tantanmen (豆乳担々麺) is a wheat-noodle dish; taco rice uses seasoned "veggie-meat" that commonly contains soy sauce/wheat; miso and standard shoyu-based seasonings (tomato miso, dressings) are wheat-fermented unless a wheat-free tamari is confirmed; no dedicated fryer is documented so the フリット and any fried item risk shared-oil cross-contact. Treat as "real GF items exist, but confirm ingredients + cross-contamination for each order" rather than safe-by-default.
tokyo3_revive_kitchen_three_hibiy.vegan_detail: The whole restaurant is meat- and fish-free ("MODERN SHOJIN"), and there is a clearly fully-vegan flagship: the seasonal ベジミールスタンド / veggie-meal stand (~¥4,290) — e.g. Brussels-sprouts borscht, shiitake soy-milk gratin, celeriac steak with romesco, root-vegetable terrine, kale & Puy-lentil salad. Other plant-based items: ten-grain veggie-meat taco rice (¥1,980), tomato-miso soy-milk tantanmen (¥2,200), spiced carrot cake, soy-milk-&-turmeric whipped desserts. HOWEVER the menu is not uniformly vegan — THREE's official page states some items contain eggs and dairy, so a vegan must specify and check per dish. Dashi: the set includes a 冬野菜のすまし汁 (vegetable clear soup); sources do not explicitly confirm it is 100% plant-based (no bonito), so flag/ask about hidden dashi. Soy milk is used widely as the dairy substitute; no egg noted in the vegan meal stand itself.

tokyo3__70.gf_detail: No GF information could be verified for this specific shop — nothing was published online, so treat everything below as unconfirmed and ask in person. As a general matter, an ordinary Japanese soba-dokoro is HIGH RISK for celiacs: (1) most "soba" here is nihachi (二八) — roughly 20% wheat flour blended into the buckwheat, so the noodles themselves usually contain wheat unless a dish is explicitly labeled juwari/十割; (2) even juwari soba is NOT safe — the tsuyu/mentsuyu dipping and soup base is made with regular wheat-based soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu), and any tempura is wheat-batter fried in shared oil; (3) buckwheat and wheat flour are milled/dusted in the same kitchen, so cross-contamination on boards, boiling water and utensils is expected. No dedicated GF kitchen or fryer is known. A celiac should not assume any dish here is safe without a direct, careful conversation (ideally with a Japanese allergy card), and realistically should treat this shop as unsuitable unless staff can specifically confirm juwari noodles AND a gluten-free tamari-based tsuyu — which was NOT documented.
tokyo3__70.vegan_detail: The listing signals "vegetarian options," but nothing vegan-specific could be verified for this shop. The critical hidden-animal risk at any soba shop is the broth: soba tsuyu, kake-soba soup and mentsuyu are almost always built on katsuo-dashi (bonito/skipjack) and often niboshi (dried sardine), so even a plain zaru/mori soba dipping sauce or a "vegetable" tempura soba is typically non-vegan. Tempura may also share oil with shrimp/fish. A vegan should ask specifically whether a kombu-only (kelp) dashi is available and whether any dish can be served without bonito — this was not confirmed. Do not assume plant-based unless staff verify the dashi.

tokyo3__104.gf_detail: No gluten-free program; the signature 18-dish breakfast is dense with wheat-risk items (wheat-containing soy sauce and miso across several dishes, tamagoyaki, mentaiko, likely-battered fried eggplant on a possibly shared fryer, and miso-soup dashi). No dedicated GF kitchen or fryer. Only okayu (plain rice porridge) and fresh fruit are inherently low-risk, but they arrive as part of a mixed set. A celiac should treat the menu as unsafe unless each item is confirmed with staff — 'ask' at best.
tokyo3__104.vegan_detail: Not a vegan/vegetarian restaurant despite the temple setting and "shojin-inspired" marketing. The signature 18-dish breakfast explicitly contains fish and meat: ikura (salmon roe) with yuba, nori-mentaiko (cod roe), octopus in shio-koji, Tsukiji Kimbun fish tofu, aigamo (duck) with sansho, plus tamagoyaki (egg). The miso soup uses standard dashi (bonito likely — hidden animal stock). No dedicated vegan menu is published. Some individual plant components exist (black beans, kombu tsukudani, soy-braised eggplant, tofu, pickles, fruit, matcha jelly), and PRONTO café drinks/sweets are available, but a fully vegan plate is not offered as such — a vegan must confirm each item and avoid the set breakfast. Flag hidden dashi/bonito in the soup and any simmered vegetable dishes.

chef_bio.background: The café is operated by PRONTO Corporation (a nationwide Japanese coffee/café chain) as an official concession inside the Tsukiji Hongwanji Information Center, opened when the center was completed in 2017. There is no single celebrity chef; the concept is a temple-grounds Japanese café. The signature 18-dish breakfast is assembled from small dishes sourced from long-established shops in the Tsukiji Outer Market rather than cooked by a named head chef.
chef_bio.philosophy: A 'temple café' concept: an accessible, tourist-friendly Japanese breakfast whose 18-small-bowl format is a nod to Buddhist/shojin aesthetics and the number of Amida Buddha's vows, presented as a calm start to the day overlooking the main hall — marketed as shojin-motif rather than strict shojin ryori.
chef_bio.specialty: 18品の朝ごはん (18-dish breakfast): 16 small side dishes plus okayu (rice porridge), miso soup and tea.

anecdotes.text: The 18-dish breakfast's small side dishes are drawn from renowned shops of the Tsukiji Outer Market (e.g., fish tofu by Tsukiji Kimbun), tying the café to the surrounding market rather than an in-house kitchen.
The breakfast is made in limited daily quantities and frequently sells out before the 10:30 end of breakfast service, so the café offers online reservations for the morning slot.

tokyo3__148.gf_detail: Effectively a dedicated gluten-free environment: the entire brand is wheat-free — no wheat flour is used anywhere in the operation. All baked goods and brunch items are built on 米粉 (rice flour from 四万十川源流の土佐れいほく米), JAS-certified oatmeal, domestic okara (soy pulp), and homemade apple yeast. The official site states products are suitable for wheat-allergy sufferers ("小麦アレルギー・卵アレルギーの方"). No tempura, no flour-dusting, no wheat soy-sauce tsuyu on premises (it is a bakery/brunch cafe, not a soba/noodle shop). CAVEAT for a strict celiac: the shop does NOT publish a formal cross-contamination protocol or third-party GF certification, and some items are co-produced with an outside welfare workshop (就労継続支援B型『ナンクルナイサァーろくえもん』) — that facility is also stated to make the vegan/GF sweets, but I could not verify its handling protocols. Oats are used (JAS oatmeal); highly oat-sensitive celiacs should ask whether the oats are certified GF-purity. Bottom line: no wheat is handled at all, which removes the primary celiac risk, but confirm oat sourcing and shared-equipment handling directly if you are highly sensitive.

No dashi/bonito concern: this is a baked-goods and brunch/bread-plate cafe, not a Japanese savory kitchen. Menu is entirely vegan: rice-flour muffins (cinnamon-roll, carrot cake, "milk"), cookies (orange-chocolate, almond, chai spice), banana bread, corn bread, carrot-spice bread, donuts, nut tarts, lemon/blueberry/kiwi cakes; drinks include Earl Grey, 日々乃コーラ craft cola, and specialty coffee from 田代珈琲. Whole facility is vegan, so no animal-product cross-contact risk.

His signature idea, 一日一膳 玄米生活 ('one bowl of brown rice a day'), centers on his 寝かせ玄米® (aged/fermented brown rice) as a complete staple food. He preaches achievable, non-perfectionist wellness — 'health at 70 points is fine' — rather than restrictive dieting, and links personal health to the health of the planet: choosing what you eat is choosing what future you want to live in.

tokyo3_gugga.gf_detail: Important: "GUGGA" the brand is wheat-flour-free (its cookies/brownies use organic oat flour, no wheat), BUT this entry is the vegan SOUP BREAKFAST served inside CLANN BY THE RIVER, an omnivore riverside café at LYURO Tokyo Kiyosumi 2F — there is no dedicated GF kitchen or fryer. (3) The same kitchen prepares Kiyosumi clam chowder and BBQ-style dishes (venue inherited the PITMANS BBQ operation), so shared-surface cross-contamination is likely. tokyo3_gugga.vegan_detail: Real, reliable vegan option: the "soup breakfast" offers a seasonal VEGAN soup as an explicit alternative to the KIYOSUMI clam chowder (the chowder contains dairy + clams and is NOT vegan). The vegan soup is produced by GUGGA, a fully plant-based sweets/recipe brand, so it should contain no bonito/dashi — but confirm the specific day's soup and side, since it is cooked in a shared omnivore kitchen. Sides are bread or rice (pick rice if avoiding egg/dairy in bread). This is NOT an all-vegan restaurant; it is an omnivore hotel café with a dependable vegan soup and GUGGA vegan baked goods.

chef_bio.chef_name: 山後静音 (Shizune Yamago) — founder of GUGGA (brand that produces the vegan soup); the on-site cook at CLANN BY THE RIVER is not documented
chef_bio.background: GUGGA was founded in 2018 in Kamakura, Kanagawa. Shizune discovered veganism while studying at university in Hawaii, where her roommates were vegan, which reshaped how she saw plant-based food. She started GUGGA without a physical shop — catering, event pop-ups and wholesale — and it grew so popular through magazine features that a one-person operation could no longer keep up. She has since relocated to Kitanakagusuku Village, Okinawa, with her husband, who runs the chocolate workshop 'SANGO Bakes and Chocolate,' where GUGGA products are now based. GUGGA has no standalone Tokyo storefront; in Kiyosumi it appears as the GUGGA-produced vegan soup at CLANN BY THE RIVER.
chef_bio.philosophy: Reconstruct the American-style home desserts her grandmother used to bake with her, using 100% plant-based ingredients — wheat-flour-free (organic oat flour), domestic unrefined kibi cane sugar, organic coconut oil — so that 'vegan eating can feel this good' as an everyday reward rather than a restriction.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan, wheat-flour-free soft cookies and sablés (flavors like espresso salted caramel, lemon-rosemary-macadamia, cranberry-chai-cacao-nib) and a 100% plant-based chocolate brownie; also develops vegan soups and recipes for partner cafés such as CLANN BY THE RIVER.

anecdotes.text: She discovered veganism as a university student in Hawaii, where all her roommates were vegan — the experience that led her to reimagine baked goods with only plant-based ingredients.

Demand outgrew what one person could bake; rather than 'stop production,' she built a network of collaborators and entrusts soft-cookie manufacturing to 'Aile Shonan,' a Type-B welfare work facility, maintaining quality through shared technical dialogue.
GUGGA has since moved from Kamakura to Okinawa (Kitanakagusuku), where products are sold at her husband's 'SANGO Bakes and Chocolate' workshop.

tokyo3__159.gf_detail: Not safe to rely on for celiac. The house specialty is 生麩 (nama-fu / raw wheat gluten), sourced from Kyoto's 半兵衛麩 — it is essentially pure wheat and appears throughout the signature dishes (生麩田楽, 生麩と季節野菜の揚げ出し, and the flagship 湯葉クリームコロッケ which packs yuba AND nama-fu into a flour-breaded, deep-fried croquette). Menu leans heavily on deep-fried items (揚げ湯葉サラダ, croquette, agedashi) with no indication of a dedicated fryer, so shared-oil and flour/panko cross-contamination is likely. Standard Japanese soy sauce and tsuyu (wheat-containing) and dashi season most dishes. A few items are naturally wheat-free in isolation (自家製豆腐, 湯葉 sashimi, vegetable obanzai) but there is no GF program, labeling, or allergen handling — a celiac should treat this as a wheat-forward kitchen. Note: any juwari/soba is not offered as a GF claim here regardless.
tokyo3__159.vegan_detail: Plant-forward but NOT a vegan/精進 restaurant — it is an omnivore washoku house that also serves wagyu (天草黒毛和牛). Genuinely plant-based components exist (湯葉 yuba sashimi/spring rolls, 生麩 nama-fu dengaku with miso, 自家製豆腐, vegetable おばんざい), but there is no vegan designation and hidden animal ingredients are very likely: katsuo (bonito) dashi in the 出汁茶漬け, ankake and simmered items; dairy/egg in the yuba cream croquette; wheat-based soy sauce. No 精進だし (kombu-only) is advertised. A vegan diner must explicitly ask each dish and request kombu dashi — do not assume the "vegetable" dishes are animal-free.

tokyo3_oh_nana.gf_detail: Genuine 100% gluten-free establishment — no wheat is used anywhere in the kitchen. The owner, Nana, has celiac disease and built the restaurant specifically so celiacs can eat every item without asking: the motto is "No need to ask — it's gluten free, all the time" (東京100％グルテンフリーレストラン). Because the whole facility is wheat-free, the usual Japanese wheat traps are removed: soy sauce/seasonings are the gluten-free type, there is no shared tempura/fry oil with wheat batter, and no flour dusting. This is one of the very few Tokyo spots a strict celiac can rely on without cross-contamination worry. No juwari/soba wheat-tsuyu concern applies here. (Verified against the restaurant's own site and Tabelog; if in doubt, staff ask about and double-check every allergy at ordering.)
tokyo3_oh_nana.vegan_detail: The restaurant's stated concept is "グルテンフリー100%・ヴィーガン対応" — gluten-free with vegan accommodation. A specific vegan menu was not published online at time of checking, and the food is Japanese-style, so hidden animal stock is the risk to flag: confirm that dashi/broths and sauces are made without bonito (katsuo), fish, or other animal products when ordering vegan. Staff proactively ask about all dietary restrictions and double-check the order, so vegan requests can be accommodated — but treat vegan dishes as made-to-request rather than a guaranteed dedicated vegan menu.

chef_bio.background: Founder and owner of Oh Nana!. She was diagnosed with celiac disease roughly four years ago and, after struggling to find safe food at restaurants, convenience stores and supermarkets across Japan, opened Oh Nana! in March 2026 — she frames it as Japan's first Western-standard, fully celiac-safe restaurant. The venue took over the site of the former organic restaurant ROSY near Kanda Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: Create an inclusive space where everyone — gluten-free or not — can share good Japanese food together and make happy memories, so that people with dietary restrictions no longer have to eat apart from family and friends. Guiding promise: 'No need to ask — it's gluten free, all the time.'
chef_bio.specialty: 100% gluten-free Japanese cuisine and café fare (lunch, café, dinner), plus gluten-free bento, gluten-free cooking classes, and a gluten-free food tour.

Her name Nana means 'seven' (a lucky number) in Japanese, and she was born on July 7th — the restaurant leans into that as a symbol of good fortune.

tokyo3__161.gf_detail: Genuinely strong GF setup for a Tokyo izakaya — but read the caveats. The house soy sauce is a gluten-free broad-bean (空豆) tamari-style shoyu, salt is Okinawan Nuchima-su, and cooking is advertised as roughly 98% non-oil on the teppan. The omakase vegetable course is described by the restaurant/Vegewel as 完全グルテンフリー (completely gluten-free), and the shop explicitly advertises accommodating グルテンフリー / ビーガン / 五葷抜き requests. It is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen: wheat lives on the premises — a Turkish simit/シミット sesame bread and a hummus set, plus an attached bakery whose ~30 breads are mostly wheat. Okonomiyaki uses 玄米・大和芋・米粉 (brown rice, yam, rice flour) as binder rather than wheat flour, but is cooked on the same teppan as bread items. A celiac should order the explicitly GF course, confirm the GF broad-bean soy sauce is used on their specific dishes, and flag cross-contact from bread/flour and the shared teppan. (No juwari-soba concern here — this is not a soba shop.)
tokyo3__161.vegan_detail: Plant-based vegetable izakaya (野菜居酒屋) with a dedicated vegan course (~¥3,500 pre-tax) and vegan-cheese (ビーガンチーズ) dishes — avocado/vegan-cheese spring rolls, vegan-cheese-baked gourd with oyster mushroom, strawberry & baby-greens okonomiyaki, hot teppan potato salad. Dashi appears plant-based (no bonito/dashi-fish mentioned anywhere) but not explicitly confirmed — worth a check. The concept is framed as letting vegans and meat-lovers dine together comfortably (ビーガンの方と肉好きの方が), so confirm any individual dish is fully animal-free; the attached bakery also includes non-vegan breads (only ~1/3 of its breads are vegan).

tokyo3_t_s.gf_detail: Not safe for a celiac. T'sたんたん is a vegan RAMEN counter and its core noodle is standard wheat 中華麺 (Chinese-style wheat noodle) — gluten by definition. The tantan/soy tare is built on ordinary Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, and the sesame-tantan base is a shared wheat-exposed kitchen. No dedicated gluten-free noodle, dedicated fryer, or gluten protocol was found for THIS Gransta Tokyo station location. tokyo3_t_s.vegan_detail: [Held at "some vegan options" 2026-08-20] The "fully vegan" label was contradicted by this record's own cited sources. Fully plant-based — this is one of Tokyo's landmark vegan ramen shops. The entire menu uses no meat, seafood, dairy, or eggs ("肉・魚介・乳製品・卵を一切使わずに"), and the broth is a vegetable/kombu-style umami base rather than bonito/animal dashi, so there is no hidden fish-stock trap that plagues most Japanese ramen. Because the whole kitchen is vegan, there is essentially no animal cross-contact risk. An "oriental veg" (no onion/garlic, allium-free) option is also available. Confirm nothing is topped with honey-style condiments if you are strict, but the shop is designed and marketed as 100% vegan.

chef_bio.background: Founder and representative of T's Restaurant. Born March 1956, a Keio University graduate. She was originally a lover of animal foods (fatty tuna toro, cream dishes) and turned to plant-based eating after a close friend fell ill and was advised by doctors to cut animal products, which crystallized her belief in preventative health through everyday food. She opened the flagship T's Restaurant in Jiyugaoka in September 2009 and created the T'sたんたん vegan-ramen spin-off, which now runs multiple locations across Tokyo train stations and Narita Airport. She is a director of the Japan Plant-Based Market Association.
chef_bio.philosophy: 'Smile Veg' (スマイルベジ) — communicate the importance of health through food that is delicious enough that anyone, vegan or not, is happy to eat it. Vegan food should be an accessible, joyful default (in schools, offices, airlines, stations), not a compromise.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan tantanmen and plant-based ramen with animal-free umami depth (no meat, fish, egg, dairy, or bonito dashi).

anecdotes.text: A former marbled-toro-and-cream lover, Shimokawa switched to plant-based cooking after a close friend became ill and doctors advised reducing animal products; she began serving her family tofu-based 'meat sauce' pasta and noticed her own mornings became lighter and more energetic.

T's Restaurant was born in a near-magical 5-day span in May 2009: a chance meeting with a photographer led to a plate designer who imagined a 'mountain-lodge-style' natural restaurant; the next day she spotted a newly built space near Jiyugaoka Station, called on impulse, and one unit was free. It opened on the 25th — a date she says kept recurring at every milestone.

Her vegan noodles were adopted as international-airline in-flight meals, and she published what is described as Japan's first home-use vegan recipe book, 『奇跡のごちそう』 (2013); her Smile Veg work has extended to corporate cafeterias and school lunches for tens of thousands of students in Tsukuba.

tokyo3_lei.gf_detail: This is a genuinely wheat-free establishment, not a place that merely offers a few GF items. The restaurant's own name and concept is 「小麦を使わない国産ビストロ」— "a domestic bistro that does not use wheat." A gluten-free blogger who visited reports the chef himself has a wheat allergy ("シェフが小麦アレルギーとのことで相談もできて安心"), so no wheat flour is used anywhere: bread and quiche/pastry are made with rice flour (米粉), and even the signature spice curry is 小麦粉不使用 (no wheat-flour roux), thickened instead with house bouillon and long-cooked whole onions. Because there is no wheat in the kitchen, the usual Japanese cross-contamination traps (tempura batter, shared fryer with breaded items, flour dusting) do not apply here. The one thing NOT independently confirmed on any source page is the soy sauce / seasoning base: ordinary Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and while a fully wheat-free bistro almost certainly uses a wheat-free tamari, a celiac should still confirm the soy sauce and any sauce/curry base directly on-site. Overall this is one of the safest-looking GF options in the Akihabara area for a celiac, precisely because the whole kitchen is built around avoiding wheat.
tokyo3_lei.vegan_detail: Vegan is not the focus — the menu centers on domestic meat and animal products: Miyagi (Oshika Peninsula) venison cooked sous-vide with beet sauce, mochi-pork ("もち豚") smoked/curry dishes, spinach quiche and chocolate terrine (egg/dairy), and a house bouillon that is very likely animal-based. There are plant-forward items (grilled seasonal vegetables, rice-flour bread), so a vegetarian or flexible diner can eat, but a strict vegan must confirm the dashi/bouillon and ask for meat- and dairy-free versions. No explicitly labelled vegan set was found. Note the GF strength here does NOT extend to vegan — treat those as separate questions on-site.

chef_bio.background: The chef is described as being from the Tohoku region and, per a gluten-free blogger, has a wheat allergy himself — which is the origin of the entirely wheat-free concept. The kanda-curry.com curry-grandprix page separately refers to a manager 「店長コバヤシさん」(Mr. Kobayashi), who may or may not be the chef; the chef's full name was not confirmed on any source, so it is left blank rather than guessed.
chef_bio.philosophy: 小麦を使わない (never use wheat) and 国産 (domestic-sourced): body-friendly cooking built on Japanese ingredients, domestic natural wine, and Tohoku produce (Miyagi venison, seasonal vegetables), using rice flour in place of wheat throughout.
chef_bio.specialty: Rice-flour bistro cooking — house rice-flour bread baked daily, wheat-flour-free spice curry (house bouillon, cardamom/cinnamon, whole domestic onions), Miyagi Oshika-Peninsula venison, and a cocoa-based gluten-free chocolate terrine, paired with domestic (Tohoku) wines.
